div.head: ARRAN MURDER.
div.p: THE ARRAN MURDER.

John Watson Laurie was formally charged at tins,- ock Sheriff Court, on Tuesday, with the murder of Edward Robot Rose, in the Isle of Arran, on tle• 15111 July last. Laurie, who appear's' wit-posse...Nl, pleaded not guilty. Ile was committed to trial at Edinburgh on the Bth November.

INCREASE IN THE WAGES OF RAILWAY MEN. The directors of the London and North-Western Rail- way Company have derided to advance the wages of their drivers and firemen on Thuoulay. Shooters wages will be advanced 3a. per week; inspect.", 2s. W.; Makesmen a graduated rise; pointsmen, Is. to 3s. ; foremen platelayers. Zn: and extra brakesmen are to be allowed time and a h.li for all Sunday work. Engineers' wages are also advanced 3s. weekly. GREAT FIRE IN A BOOT FACTORY-

I The large boot and shoe manufactory of Messrs. I Bradshaw and Payne, Lumberstontsroad, Leicester, was wholly detroved by fire on Tuesday, the damage I amounting to £al,ooo. The place was just being reopened for work after (HMV, when thetie. burst imt of ftto s orkrno rn , and the operatives had to flee for their lives. The fiances burned very fiercely, and ,veral I adjoining factories were in great danger. Atssit 300 I hands are thrown idle.

div.head: FATAL RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT DA RESEU It Y.
div.p: FATAL RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT DA RESEU It Y.

A shocking accident occurred to Mr. Hayward, wheelwright, who arrived at Daresbury Station late on Momlay evening. It appears that is is a I practice for residents in the neighbourhood of Daresbitry, on arriving by tram, to proceed along !the line. Strong warnings had been given by the stationmaster to offenders. In the case in quest ion Mr. Hayward was met at the station by his son.who wished his father to go home by the road. This, however, he ref nsed to do, and slipped down the I embankment on to the line, unobserved by the rail- way servants, the son going home by the safer route. On arriving there, and his father not put- ' ting in an appearance, lie went in search of lore. . and the unfortunate man was ultimately found on the line terribly injured. Intelligence was at ones • conveyed to Warrington, and medical ail sought. Mr. Reginald Smith loon of Dr. Starkey Smith) and Mr. Gyton (assistant) were immediately conveyed by special train to Daresbury, but only to hind that all aid was unavailing. The top of the poor fellow's head had been cradled off by a passing train.

SATURDAY. NOVEMBEW 2. 1689.

Mr. Madatono IT must have been pleas,nt it at Mr. ILIUMTONE to turn from the s.4altncv. . - strife and the din. of polities—inevi- table to they are—to the pilot aud yet lofty re- view of social progress, which he tuidertook at Fanner, on Saturday. The speech is one of the best, as it is certainly one of the mostanteresting he . has ever made. It may be said of him 113811AKES- reass said of CLEOPATRA—age cannot wither hint Inor custom stale his infinite, variety. It is usual Ifor his political opponents to seer:, for 54,-ns in hix • ! speeches indicative of the failing mental power which often accompanies old age, amid they are I pram to say they see evidences, of it when he dis- cusses Home Rule.. But they are not wholly impartial judges on such an issue; and they ought rather to be invited to express opinion on the merits of such an address as that delivered at the opening of the Saltney Literary Institute. What a wide range of subjects was touched! And yet each was adorned with its pearl of observation, of comment, or of fact. It is indeed true, 89 Mr. GLADSTONE remarked at the outset, that old age makes people talkative. It is nature: for them to live in the poet, rather than look for' I ward to the future; and this was upecially noticeable in the late Mr. Hamar for many years before his death. But it is not characteristic of the leader of the Liberal party. His mind iv, of that wonderfully expansive kind that it.can yet look forward with eagerness and alertneu as it did a generati,n ago. Still, it can look back when OCORSIOR requires, RP it WAS required at SiLltriOy, and the moult is a species of talkativeness which we might well wish would go on for over. It is a pertinemtt. retain& r,when there are people who have their niagivings it to the wisdom of Free Educe- tion,that there was • time when sit was certainly considered by vcry many men to hi- a very doubt- ful question indeed whether it was at all desirable upon, any terms and conditions to found veers primary schools for the working-men of the coon- try..to open to them the first steps in the acquisi- tion, of knowledge." Human nature in the lump cre regarded as so had that to give it further power was not to augment the happiness or , virtue of niankind, but to increase the sickest' Buss of the world. This is not the view now I taken an to education, after 70 years' of experi- ence ; lint a similar feeling is at the bottom of very much of the opposition to Home Rule for Ireland. Mr. GLADETOI4II took oosision to refer to the change of feeling which had come over the work' • ing-clasaes with regard to machinery. The iron horse is a tireless and uncomplaining animal; and it has so lessened human physical toil in almost every department of industry, that it is now every- where welcomed as a benefactor. That the work- ing-classes have henefitted along with other classes by the introduction and the marvellous extension of machinery, no one can deny; but they have not benefitted no much u the classes above them; and the great problem of the age is to provide for a greeter dilfmion of the enormous wealth which through the enormous use Of Steam power and
even and told, the natik

mie.l Ty is year by year accumulating in civi- lised communities. Referring to other evidence of prorrens, Mr. Gt.* mirosa said :—"Life is lengthened ; life is inure healthy than it was. The range I d disease and physical suffering among the people in narrowed.- And yet it is not to be denied that three bleasings are less at the command lof the p.r than they are of the rich. The mortality am(,ng. the children of the poor is double that of the children of the rich ; while Parliament is, for the Intel part, as indifferent to the causes of this Ilisparity as though it related to swine rather than human lain4A. Indeed, we might say more indifferent, for if there happened to be a consider- able increase of swine fever it is more than prob- chic that the 4:overnment would he inundated with questions oil Ow subject. There is something :If course that twople inust do for themselves, and Mr. I: LA iscroNe was careful to lay emphasis on the value of thrift and self-reliance lie had a useful word to say Olt the dignity of manual labour ; and.
concluding a delightful addreati, he referred in the , following exalted terms to the higheet purposee of adueation : -

No doubt you are to seek the knowledge which is useful for the temporal purposes of life, but never forget that the purpose for whieb man lives it the improvement rd the man himself.--( Hear, hear.) It IA in order that he may go nut of this world having, ai be hopes, in a great sphere or in a small one, done some little good to bit fellow-creatures, laboured a little to diminish the sin and the sorrow that are in the world and that deface what would otherwise be its fair and lovely countenance, for his own growth. bin own development, to bring him- self up to the full capacity of WO nature. This, and not the mere taking in of what is called useful knowledge in order to oleal it out again, is the great and supreme purpose ot education.

I,t LORI, HARTINGTON sticks stolidly Ilartisoen'A to his position--that of inflexible Argument. opposition to Home Rule und he gets as singry as it is imasible for his lord- ship to get at the idea id bracketing English re- forms with the propmell b. give a national Parlia- ment b. Ireland. Speaking at Wolverhampton, ,lon Tlloolll3', he said

If the people of this country cared also, as he doubted not a great many of them lit, for questions such us Disestablishment, such as free education, such as {emperance legislation, and a hundred other subjects which he cool,' now. Md they think so little of tile justice. and the right, and the expe-; diency of tic' cense and the policy in which they o were engaged in advocating that these things would ; unt come{ in their due and proper season r In other words, Englishmen having committed ! thtemelves to Home Rule, t not have any { other jobulk ol their platform! Such a Boggess ; lion --Hoch an al word suggestion—shows how tom- pletely the member for Roasenolode has lost touch with English Liberalism. He hots noot only coastal to look ahead himself, but he has begun to be stirs ; prised that anybody else should look ahead. Has ; he forgotten as to Scotch Disestablishmont, that { he himself laid down the principle that it was a ~,,otter for the people of Scotland themselves to de- termine r And if the principle applies to Scotland, it applies too England and to Wales —not only as to Disestalolishment, but as to the question of Home I Rule. At to Free Education, Lord HARTING- TON surely kmows that that is now practically within the grasp of the people of Scotland. It has been wrung from an unwilling Parliament I even while Home Rode has been under discussion ; awl now we on this side of the border are to ho told, forsooth, that we have is right to push it to ! the front whilst the Irish question is before the ioatio on. Really, Lord HA KTINGTON Mat have ; closed lois eyes as to what is going on around him: !I he is the Rip Van Winkle who has gono to sleep son Irish bog. Referring to tho difficulty which might arise through Irish members having one seat in Dublin, and another at W.tininister, his lordship thus states his objection :

It was not in the power, he Aid, of any person to frame a scheme of Rome Rule for Ireland which shonld include the retention of the Irish members in the Imperial Parliament which would not have one of flies., two consequences -either the necessity of breaking up our own Parliament and our Govern- ment, and the creation of a new Parliament and 0 new Government for the management of our in- costal affairs, which would be a constitutional change of the most tremendous description, or in the other ease that moult place England in the absurd and humiliating position of having its own internal government chosen for by members coming from a country over whose government we had no control. In 1110 opinion the retention of the Irish members at Westminster was incompatible with ! any scheme for the future government of Ireland which should proceed on the basis of the nationality of a national Parliament. There is nothing new in this argument against HOMO Rule, but it is, we grant, very forcibly put. Lord iIiRTISIOTON, however, himself points to the way unit of the difficulty when he talks of "a new Parliament and a new Government for the man-1 agetnent of OM internal affairs." It is true he trim to frighten people by describing it as "a constitu- tional change of the most tremendous des- cription " ; but Liberals are not to he frightened , by big words. They need only to convince I themselves that what they propose to do is I the hest thing to do, all circumstances con- airforce], tool then set tibia doing it. It in practically settled that we are to have Home Rule for Ireland, and already there is a demand for Home Ride in Scotland, in Wales, and in England. Let Lord HARTINOTON, or any other Dissentient, or Tory, who happenti to be troubled as tin what is to be done with the Irish members, imagine for a moment what is likely to happen, namely, the eetabliahment nsf fonr anbordinate Parliamenta for domestic affairs, teal one Imperial Parliament for Imperial affairs : teal then ask if that does not settle the issues raiserl in a reasonable and effective way. It may seers to politicians of the timid school a" tremendous " thing to do ; but it would b., nothing like SO tremendous as the great reforms etrectml by Mr. GLelleitnONE in the glorious Adminis- tration which hinted from lietB to 1874—the Ad- ministration which gave us National Education, and vote by Ballot, which disestabliehed the Irish Church, tied abolished purchase in the Liberals are not to Is, frighened by any amount of croaking, however loud it may lie. They are used to it ; there Ime been crushing ever since there were fnigs in Egypt ; and the creaking is always loudest when some great, wise, and beneficient change is about to be effected in the intereets of the people.

div.head: " TOUCD AND GO."
div.p: " TOUCD AND GO."

Messrs. Mactnillan and Co. have hit the public . fancy by their sixpenny edition of Kingsley's "Westward Ho !" The demand has risen from 100,000 to 300.000, and the printers cannot keep pace with the demand. Happy printers and happy publishers!

! The "World" says:--" I hear that the Queen will probably open Parliament in person, in co impliance : with Lord Salisbury's earnest wish: No doubt Lord Salisbury does wish it ; hut it does not look well, when he is losiiig gr mind with the country, to say to the Queen "Come overand help us." Rather than make such an appeal, Mr. Gladstone would resign a dozen times. It is suggestive of the march of events that there , was a time when the Rouse of Lords made merry over the proposals of Lord Teyuham, who has just died. He used to bring forward math measures as a Ballot Bill, and a Bill for the Extension of the Franchise. Very funny, 110 doubt, " long, long ago," but how does it look sow? Lord Teynham, as an advanced Liberal, lived to see it practically acknowledged by the peers that the sense was on his side and the stupidity on theirs,

Alderman Harrison, unlike some of tho Conser- vative leaders, showed that he had the courage of his convictions by attending the meeting, on Tues- day evening, in support of Liberal candidates when he had been party to bringing them into the field. The Mayor too, wrote is straightforward letter mid would have been present if he could. Councillor Jenkins was present: he, too, is a Con- servative; and he lot the nail on the head when he said Messrs. Platt and Roberto had been assailed in a most dishonounible manner.

The Tory agent tries to draw is distinction be- tweLm Conservative leaders acting as members of the Town Council and members of the Tory party. ' But he does not succeed; it in an attempt to make , straight that which is decidedly crooked. Alder- man Fraucomb is, for iivitmie, chairman of the very ward in which Messrs. Platt and Roberts have been opposed. Would Mr. Hainpson have people believe that, when Alderman Francomb assured the retiring Councillors that if they would stand agaio they would not he oppoaed, he had 110 authority to speak as a Conservative? A chair- man of a ward is usually thought to he somebody; the Tory agent would make him out to he nobody.

The attempt of the Tory ring to whiten their black conduct with the plea that a labour candi- date, whom a Liberal, had entered another ward, is an utter failure, in view of the fact, as stated by Mr. Platt, that it was well known the labour candidates were selected when he and Mr. Frank Roberts were solicited by the Tory leaders to allow themselves to lie nominated. The Tory wire- pullers have been guilty of a shabby trick—a trick which it is something to be able to say, is openly denounced by the more respectahle leaden of their own party.

But shabby tricks, like chickens and curses, come home to roost. The electors have shown that, in their judgment, they believe honesty is the best policy—in polities, as in everything else. They have triumphantly returned Messrs. John Platt and Frank A. Roberts. The Liberal candi- dates have won a victory, notwithstanding that they were late in the field and unprepared for aeon- test. The boast was that Mr. Platt could be de- feated, and the electors have answered this boast by placing him at the head of the poll.

A theatrical divorcee's. had a theatrical hearing at the Divorce Court on Monday. An actor named Blake made on, it seems, with the wife f Mr. K Storey, who is also an actor. Blake had made it known to the husband that ho was "very fond " of the nmaway wife, and wee " not such a Johnny as to leave her." But the husband was equal to the tweasion, for "he thanked the respon- dent for taking such a wife from him." The divorce was granted ; and "Airs well that ends I well."

Mr. Chanilmrlain seems to have found he wont too far in committing himself, off-hand, to the en- dowment of an Irish Catholic University ; and at Birmingham the other evening he heat a retreat. The fact is, he is like the Tories ; he has discovered that it won't do. The Irish Secretary, writing thie week to the Rev. Dr. lk.th, in acknowledgment of a resolution against the proposed endowment says—•' The quostion ia at present hardly ripe for discussion." Mr Balfour is right for once; it is not ripe—it is sour, very emir.

div.p: 'IRON TRADE. GREAT ADVANCE IN PRICES

' During the past week or two prices of Cleveland i pig iron have sheen rapidly advancing, hut they , have never bounded up at such a rate as they did ,on Monday at Middlesbrough. Quotations cow- ' menced to improve slowly in the early port of the • day, but later on they advairiel very quickly. and , the market rioted with Cleveland No. ,l pig iron ,30. Ni. per ton attire prices realised last week, mak- ing Cleveland iron only Ild, below the quotations ' for Scotch. There was a steady rise to 5.55., but on information from Glasgow to the effect that war- rants in the Scotch centre were bounding up at a grout rate being received the Middlesbrough market became very exciter), and sellers refused to accept lens than Mk iht. per ton for No 3 Cleveland. The , great advance has certainly ton very considerable !extent been brought about by speculation, but at the same time there is a good steady bond fide , demand. Shipments of pig iron from Middles- brongh continue excellent, and stocks are still being rapidly reduced. On Monday night Messrs. Connal held at Middlesbrough a stock of 162,821 tons of pig iron, being a decrease on the week of no less than 5,275:t0.. Prospects for the future are , bright and encouraging. On Wednesday excitement ; existed in the Staffordshire iron trade, resulting , from the extraordinary movements in the Cleve- land and Scotch markets. Pig-iron prices were almost wholly withdrawn, sellers of Midland sorts being utterly unable to quote. Such millers as did quote asked 665. to 775. for Derbyshire, an *trance of 4s.- and 80e. for Hematites. What , figures the excitement will lead to it is impossible to see. A syntem of train lighting by electricity, (ma new nrinciple, has lieen introduced by the Cheshire Lines Committee. In other syntems the electricity is xenerally by a donkey-engine attached to the locomotive drawing the train. In the system which was tried, and tried succewfully, on Saturday on the !Cheshire Linen, the electricity is generated its the brake van. It is what is known an Radcliffe's ~ys,oll. ,011. Itlld it liar been adopted by the (treat Northern Railway Company. A dynamo is fixed in the brake . van, and it is driven by means of a stout leather belt, which pacS,M through the Hoer an.l round the axle of the vehicle. Thin in known as Radcliffe's patent automatic friction gearing. It is so arranged that the dynamo always revolves in one end the same direction, no matter which way the train is travelling. ror the portion!, of nmint.i”ing !he light during the stoppages, a net of accumulators aro prwidwl, and these are a twomat Wally connected by means of a nwit eh with, the dynamo. Two glow lamps are litted in the paneln of the carriage MlT- head. efteil being of eight candle power, and these are encored in lamps of a larger sine. The tirst train titted with the electric light on this new principle ran through Warringt on, on Sat urday,from Liverpool to Manchester.

The river will of the Ship Canal 1Y gradually drawing nearer and nearer to the ferry slip, and yet it cannot be gathered from the re (1,1118 01 the proceedings of the Board that Runcorn Commis- sioner. are taking any steps to preserve the ancient right of crossing the year. When the Ship Canal is made the public of Runcorn ought to have facilities equal to those at present enjoyed for crossing the Mersey and it is for the local legislators to act for them it the matter. The Company have made cer- tain proposalu for carrying on the ferry, but tbe Widnes Local Board strongly disapprove of them and are oppen.ing the plans being carried out. It would be interesting to learn the opinion of the Runcorn Commissioners on the subject. The formation of the Salt Union caused many landowners in the vicinity of Northwich to pierce the crust of the earth in the hope of coming across a bed of the precious white crystal era spring of brine, and in several cases success rewarded their efforts, but the all devouring Union has swallowed ' them up. A shaft has now bees conk to a depth of SO yards on the estate of the Taibots, at Aston 11511, and specimens of capital rock salt have . been brought to the surface, and there is every in- dication that a rich vein ha, hero struck upon. This will be good nowu to the Widnes chemical manufacturers, who 00' an enormous pr unity of the material in the c. Oars. if; lie year, awl they will be glad to have it so much nearer their works than Northwich.

Typhoid fever still afflict+ the populations of Run- corn and Widnes to all alarming extent and the only re-assuring fact is that the sanitary authorities appear to he taking measures for preventing the spread of the dread disease. run advantage has been taken of the Infectious Diseases Hospital at : Widn, by tie Local Board of that town, and it : would have been well NO the Runcorn Corn- ' missioners made use of the similar establishment I they possess under the shelter of Runcorn HU The costly inst it ut ion is idle, however, and the ; mtepsyem vain:y guess at the cause. An explanation ought to be forthcoming on Thursday next.

More deep is the sympathy with the , bereaved parents, because the fever scourge ban robbed them of four children within reeent years. 1 The compromise of the Widnes Scho at Board election still forms a subject of animatedl discussion in Nonconformist circles and occasionally some hard things are said. We regret to record the death of Mr. William Dutton, WiliCh took place at Birkdale. Sontliport,on Tuesday. Mr. Dutton was head of the large drapery firm of Messrs.. J. & W. Dutton.Sankey-at., Warring- ton, and until about two years agn Inc resided at Latelifonl, but at that time he removed to Birkdale, Southport, for the benefit of his health, which had begun to fail. The cause of death was inflammation of the lungs. The deceased gentleman was sixty years of age. and lie leaves a family of three son,, and four daughters. Mr. Hinton did not take any , active part in political or municipal affairs, but he held a prmtinent place among local Wesleyans, and Inc filled many important office, in connection with that denomination, Ile was also for some time one of the overseers of Latchford. _ . .

--.-.... ..... The funetal took place on Friday afternoon at Daresbury. The body was brought by train from Southport to the Central station at M arrington and was thence conveyed in a hearse to Daresbury. The coffin was covered with many hand4ome wreaths, Following the hearse were seven carriages contain- ing, amongst others, the following Messrs. J. F. Dutton, W. Dutton, Walter Dutton. J . Young, T. Dutton (Kingsley), J. Dutton ( Woodhouses), D. Dutton, Andrews (Peterborough 1, James Fairclough, John Fairclough, R. Fairclough, H. Fairclough, J. N. Dutton (Liverpool), J. Butterworth (Manchester), Balharry ( Ilaydock ), Grime (Warrington Hignett, and Dunbabin. The private carriages of Dr. Fox, and Mr. 1. Tunstall also formed part of the funeral procession. At the church the coffin was borne by six of the assistants, namely, Messrs. Bayley, Boyle, Simkinson, l'attimon, Sadler and Richardson. At i the burial service the Rev. Canon Whitley officiated. I The arrangements for the funeral were in the hands of Mr. E. Connor, of Sankey-st.. and were satisfactorily carried out by Mr. Dunbabin.

Fowls Is rag (UM/FN.—William Walker, Howley, sued Joseph Forster and George Platt, Howley Cottages, for the recovery of 10s. from each, for damages said to have been done bv their fowls to his garden produce. The plaintiff said that on several occasions the defend- ants fowls had been in his garden, and had ruined a thousand celery plants, a quantity of savoys, and a large quantity of saint—Mr. Arthur Browne defended, and contended that the damage could not be ascer- tained, inasmuch a.. 4 the plaintiff's own fowLs and goats had been in the garden. Several witnesses wetv called, , who stated that they had seen a goat and other peoples fowls in the ganlan.—llis Honour, in giving judgment, said that it was difficult for him to say whether the damage had heen done by the defendants' fowls. DESERTING WIVES AND FAMILIES Yesterday morring, us the Warrington Police Court, a man named William Caldwell was brought up on a charge of having deserted his wife and live children, on the 16th August last.--Mr. Shearer,l inquiry officer, who told the particulars of the case to the magistrates. said that prisoner had been four times dealt with for having assaulted his wife. It was also stated that one at the children was almost: in a dying contlition.--Alderman Harrison said that he wished the Bench had power to send Caldwell to prison for twelve MORIN. and to give him twenty- five lashes in addition. That was what such a fellov! as he deserved. Sentence of imprisonment for a term of three months, with hard labour, was then passed.--At the same sitting of the Court man named James Leigh was charged with having deserted his • ife. Mr. A. Browne, who appeared for the complainant, said that the parties were married in 1542, at St. Paul's church, and lived to- ' nether until about nine years ago, when the wife was compelled to leave the defendant in consequ- ence of the ill-treatment that lie subjected her to. Since then she had hail to support herself and her family, which included an invalid son. He formerly worked for Mr. Crostield, at whose instigation be allowed his wife Ills. a week for some time, but lie had now ceased to pay anything. Defendant said that lie was now out of work. The tnagistrates ordered him to contribute Os. Gd, a week towards the maintenance of his wife, at the same time intim- ating that the order would probably be increased at a future period.

div.p: Ittter6 to the Obttor.

SATURDAY EVENING ENTERTAIN MENTS." have noticed mine letters in your recent issues, relative ti the above entertainments, winch have just commenced in Rottermarket-st. schoolroom. I thomughly endorse the statementi made by the previous gentlemen, and may I remark that I, for one, hail this good object with all joy. I firmly believe such mmtings so them have been a want long felt by the working-classes of Warrington. Where has the working-man to go on the Saturday night? I adroit there an places of amuse- ment, but they are of that low order which dote more harm than good, while there are others of a better class hut the prices are a little too high for the working-man to Pay. Reverting to my former statementdet any person walk from Market-gate down Ruttermarket-st. as far as Orford-st., and they will pass no less than twelve public- houses, at which there are various sorts of questionable amusement provided for the people. Often you will bear the drunken hiccough, and the sounds of idiotic laughter, and from Riese places we see fair young men and maidens mining out. Surely something ought to be done to alleviate the great evil, and lain glad that the good friends at Buttermarketet. have commenced a counter-attraction. They have laid hold of a capital plan, which I can say, without a doubt, will the means of doing a vast amount of good. The concerts of the previous weeks have been of a refined anti purely in- teresting character, and do credit to those who have the arrangements in hand. Let me not forget to mention that the entertainment is made "moot' cheerful by tine beautiful refreshments provided. A cup of hot coffee for jil. or Id. that will do any one working-man more good than 50 glaswe of ale at lid. a glass. Eatables also, of the best deserilgion, and at reasenable prices, are supplied. I wish the projectors of tine scheme every success, as regards the attendance, because the programmes pre- pared are worthy of a full room.—Yours, " AN APPROVER."

div.head: PROTEST.
div.p: A PROTEST.

Sir, —I protest against clergymen witholding evening Communion. Whatever plea they urge, beyond doubt it was instituted in the evening, and if our Saviour par- I took of the same after his resurrection it was in the evening ; likewise Paul two years after writing to the Corinthians. I protest against clergymen assuming such 1 lordly power over the teachers and managers of Sunday schools. I protest against monkery, compelling curaten! to be colibat., to live with vicars, to the detriment of 1 pail:4ll,as competent men would not subinitto such terms, not scriptural. I protest against ltom.h Hymns being selected out of' Ancient and Modern." 352 verse 2 owns Judas from whom these men claim Apostolic succession. Whately, Wesley, Barrow, Alford all random n this dogma. 1 pmtestamainst popish 'dogmas of regeneration and transubstantiation being taught through the 'sacraments, or grace given in them. The sixth article says—. Holy Scripture contains all things necisuary to salvation, no ' that what is not read therein is riot to be thought mini- site to salvation.- Perhaps some of these sham papists will tell me one verse where infant baptism is, or con- firmation. Several of the lads who were confirmed here on last occasion are ignorant of who examined them; have never been spoken to since by any of the clergy; do not know how ninny articles there are, or the differ- ence between evening serviceand cominunion ; numbers, irrespective of soundness in doctrine, appear to suffice, an long as it will please the bishop. 1 protest against clergy turning their backs during any part of the service; it is an insuit,contrary to Rubric before Nicene erred, COMPS from Popery of the 13th century ; it implies Christ is localized on the altar, opposes the Creeds and John fourth chapter, verse twenty four ; worship in spirit, i.e., truly. I protest against paying homage to clergy when processions march up and down the church. Here after morning prayer on the first Sunday in each month 5011110 few people stand to the choir only. " The rich and the poor meet together, the I,rd is the maker of them all." I protest against floral decorations, cmsses.crucifixes, images, not scriptural, not agreeable to Article 35,0 r to Paul's advice to the Corinthians, that ye may attend upon the Lord without distraction." Prodsham, Oct. 29, 1889.

On the rampage, Pip ; on the rampage, old chap."— Marten It eta .• Those whom the gals wo:ll.l.lentroy they Ant make mat Sir.—l adopt Mr. Peers' unotation I. appropriate to thepresent discumim. On reading his letter in your last issue, you can cane to no other conclusion than that, instead of being saved from his friends, he should I I he saved by his friends. The iinpression that his letter : leaves on the mind is that he needs looking after. He 1 maintains, on the authority of Adam Clarke, that Dives was a respectable man, had plenty of money, kept a splendid table, a good cellar, invited his friends and treated them well, to that they mimml him sadly when he was removed, and was elctited in the finest productions of the loom. The only inference that can he drawn from Mr. Peers' dmluctions in this, that the Almighty com- mitted an act of injustice by consigning Dives, a res- pectable man. to a place of torment, and placing I Lanarus, who wm a scamp—a "beggar, shiftless, and , thriftleas" in heaven. Adam Clarke has not gone to far as this. I have read but little of Adorn Clarke's writ- ings, but I have mad that the late Robert Hall ;mid ' that they that they were "lb., in continent flf mud." I I have also read that in his comment on the fall and temp- tation of Eve, the doctor did not think it watt sen pent, but a being of the monkey specim that tempted Eve, and that the late Rev. Rowland Hill, noticing this inane of his sermons, told his hearers—. if you don't repent, Adam Clarke's monkey will have you." I think that Adam Clarke's monkey has been playing tricks with Mr. Peers, and the result is a continent at mud. Ile depncates the Sunday School as an institu- tion for false and erroneous teaching. llow does he know ? Is Peers among the prophets ? Ile knows as little of Sunday SCIIOOI teaching as lie does of geology. The teachings of Hugh Miller and Professor Hitchcock on the geological bearings of Genesis are more reliable than the teaching of Mr. Dors, who writes dogmati- cally, confidently, and Dannelly. lie reminds me of the Irishman who mid, "I'd pepper yees mid laming." He would have us ignore Moses, and ;Wont Mrs. Ragosin ; scout Paul, and stick to Peers. " We are about throwing off the raga of a traditional superstition," saya Mr. Peers. Who are the "We " ? Is it tho Edi- 1 halal, or the Royal " We" that lie assumes? The mania inflated beyond measure. Does to not know that the circuladon of the Scripture io greater to-day than it ever was, in 700 languages and dialects, and that millions of every section and colour of the human race believe and rely on theta as the message of God to man, and that they pmfer what Mr. Prim on contemptuously calls "the lags of a traditional superstition" as amok, beaming deem—more comfortable and congenial to honmn wants mut man's needs more in harmony with the will of had and the welfare of man. present and future, than the cold dark Garment nf Atheism.—l am, sir, yours, Ac.. div.head: MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.
div.p: THE MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.
_THE_POLLING YESTERDAY.

.... The polling for the election of members of the Corporate body, which took place yesterday, passed off in a manner even more quiet than is usually the case with municipal contests in Warrington. In two of the wards, Latchford, which returns one member, and the North-west Ward, which sends two, a poll was avoided. In the first case Mr. Tinsley, the retiring member, was the only candidate nominated, and for the other ward mentioned the two retiring members, Messrs. F. Monks and J. Greening, were elected unopposed, Mr. John Roberts, who had been also nominated, with- drawing at the last moment, and electing to devote the whole of his energies to the work of fighting another ward— the North-east. It had at first been understood that the retiring members, Messrs J. Platt and F. A. Roberts, in consequence of an arrangement that was arrived at by the Town Council at a private meeting, would have had no trouble in the matter, but when they unexpectedly, and at the eleventh hour, found that they were to he opposed, they naturally decided to stick to their guns. The Conservat iv: nomination of Messrs. W. D. Jeans and John Roberts came us a surprise, not only to the retiring members, but to the public at large. Messrs. Platt and F. A. Roberts were offered the alternative of inducing a labour candidate, with whose candidature they had nothing to do, to withdraw. on which condi- lion they would be unopposed, but they quickly came to a determination that it was not for them ' to interfere. From a report in another column of meeting of the Liberal candidates, which was pre- . sided over by a Conservative alderman, it will be seen that the action of those who were responsible for the nomination of Messrs. John Roberts and Jeans, has not met with general approval, even of the Tories. A persual of letters that were read by Mr. F. A. Roberts, and of the speeches that were maduwill provide the reader with a fuller explana- tion.

In the South-west Ward the Labour Electoral Association brought out Mr. Dunbohbin against Mr. Heaton, retiring member, and Mr. J. SI itir,while Mr. , niggle accepted nomination under the same auspices for the South-meet Ward, where he opposed Messrs. Connell, retiring member, and R. T. Fairclough. In !these two wards the candidates seemed content to let the electors have the matter pretty much to themselves, for they did not consider it necessary to address any public meetings. The poll yesterday opened at eight o'clock in the morning, and closed at the same hour in the even- ing. after which the ballot boxes were conveyed to the Town Hall. Hero the papers were counted, those for the North-east Ward in the Mayor's Parlour, and those for the South - east and South-west Wards in the Council Chamber. In the earlier part of the day the poll officials had a slow time of it. Up to noon votes came in slowly at all the booths; there was a bit of a rush at some of the stations during the workingmen's dinner hour, but in the afternoon things again dropped to a dull level. From six o'clock to closing time, of course, saw an improve- ment in this respect, and the officials then began in earnest to labour for their fees. This was especially the else in districts where the working-class voters preponderate. During the day several of the can- didates visited the polling stations, bat Mr. P. A, Roberts and Mr. R. Heaton were confined to their hoot.ea through illness.
